query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: The elemental, phase composition and microstructure of the surface of the considered HEAs, NiCoFeCr and NiCoFeCrMn, are resistant to irradiation with helium ions (40 keV, 2 × 1017 cm−2), as no formation of new phases or surface erosion was found. Thus, the main changes resulting from the irradiation of the samples are associated with the formation and interaction of radiation defects, as well as the formation and redistribution of stresses in alloys.

In the present study, the structure and phase stabilities of HEAs under ion irradiation are studied. A well studied HEA system, AlxCoCrFeNi, is chosen as a model system. Three different Al contents, x = 0.1, 0.75 and 1.5, of which structures are single fcc, fcc plus ordered bcc (B2) and B2 plus disordered bcc (A2), respectively, are employed. The microstructures of the three HEAs irradiated with Au ions are studied and compared with each other. Due to the multiple alloying elements, precipitation and phase separation could occur, which will appreciably change the structure and composition of HEAs and result in the degradation of mechanical properties, such as embrittlement. Therefore, the comparison of irradiation responses is focused on precipitation behavior. The experiment results are also compared with the conventional alloys and discussed based on theory of irradiation-induced/enhanced precipitation which is widely used in immiscible binary systems. The aim of current study is to investigate the structural stability of HEAs under ion irradiation and explore the microstructure and chemical composition dependences of irradiation tolerances of HEAs.

In contrast to conventional alloys, SP-CSAs are composed of two to five-principal elements in equal or near-equal molar ratios that form random solid solutions in either a simple face-centred cubic (f.c.c.) or simple body-centred cubic (b.c.c.) crystal lattice structure. The complicated random arrangement of alloying elements and local chemical environment at atomic level lead SP-CSAs to exhibit extraordinary properties compared with traditional alloys, such as high thermal stability and hardness, high strength-to-weight ratio, high-temperature strength, great wear and fatigue resistance, and also excellent corrosion resistance. In addition, the high-level site-to-site lattice distortions and compositional complexities in SP-CSAs can effectively reduce the mean free path of electrons, phonons and magnons; these distortions and complexities can also be used to modify formation energies, migration barriers and diffusion pathways of irradiation-induced defects, thereby modifying defect generation, interaction, interstitial–vacancy recombination in the early stages of irradiation. cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Irradiation Defects of the MEAs
cited_evidence.text: The irradiated samples did not include any holes or radiation-induced segregation (RIS). Materials exposed to radiation at doses greater than 1 dpa frequently include voids because irradiation-induced vacancies consolidate into stable cavities. Dimensional expansion and a reduction in fracture toughness are two effects of voids. It is believed that radiation-induced segregation, which occurs when alloying elements segregate out of equilibrium near sinks, is a key cause of irradiation-assisted stress corrosion cracking. As a result of the severe lattice distortion in the Three MEAs, irradiation-induced defects may diffuse slowly, inhibiting the growth of defect clusters, and defect annihilation may take place during the transition from amorphization to crystallization under conditions of high atomic-level stress.
